utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could we have -- could you call the case, please. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted for the Prosecution joined by Matthew Gillett; Case Manager, Thomas Laugel; and our intern, Maggi Qerimi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness can be brought in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Brigadier Wilson. May I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Olmsted, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Brigadier Wilson.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to begin by clarifying a couple of matters from yesterday. First, yesterday, and this is at transcript page 7449, I asked you whether it was ever envisioned that UNPROFOR would perform law enforcement in the UNPAs. And the transcript records your answer as: "No, there was some approximately 300 police within UNPROFOR and their role was to liaise, work with, supervise, assist the local police force but not to actually carry out police function within the UNPAs." Could you tell us, what did you mean by the word "supervise"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a more accurate word would be "to observe." Supervise suggests some authority. They had no authority over the local police whatsoever. They were simply there to observe, report, and hopefully positively influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could have on the screen, P2795. This is tab 56. Brigadier, this is a daily sitrep report dated 3 November 1992 which you were shown yesterday. And if we could turn to page 2. You will recall that I drew your attention to the potential heavy weapons violations at Erdut bridge listed under item 1 for Sector East. And you testified that to be certain whether this was a violation of the double-lock system you would have to -- to take a look at a map, and that was certainly a justifiable answer. If we could turn to page 5 of this document. Here is a map entitled active and potential active areas, Sector East. And we can see in the upper right mention of the weapons at Erdut bridge. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can follow the line down to the map, and perhaps zoom in a little bit where it ends. Yes. We see there's a circle indicating the spot where the violations or the weapons were -- were located. Could you tell us, is this spot inside Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And it would represent a clear violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have on the screen P2794, which was -- is tab 118. This is the historical background document you looked at yesterday. And if we could turn to page 2, and if we could look at the -- the five steps that are listed under paragraph 6, I believe. We see that the first step is the withdrawal of artillery, mortars and tanks to areas 30 kilometres outside the UNPAs. Did this requirement apply to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It applied to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if the JNA maintained artillery in Serbia but within 30 kilometres of the Sector East border, was that a heavy weapon violation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's ambiguous. I believe that it would be ignored basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It would be ignored by --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the UN. It would be -- technically it's within the 30 kilometres, but because it's in the sovereign territory of Serbia, I don't know that that would apply in that case. I could be wrong but that's my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did the UN observers, Military Observers, that you commanded, did they have access into military installations in Serbia along the border with Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not. Nor was it intended that they do in the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, at the end of the day yesterday, you testified about the special police that operated in the UNPAs after the withdrawal of the JNA. I'd like to show you a document, 65 ter 13 -- 1307. This is tab 49. This is an UNPROFOR weekly situation assessment dated 7 October 1992. And if we could look under item 3 for Sector East, it states: "Regional militia in uniforms with RPG-18 APCs, 82-millimetre mortars, et cetera." Could you tell us, what is an RPG-18?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a shoulder fired anti-tank weapon. It's considered to be a light anti-tank weapon. Can be used against other targets; for example, fortified positions, buildings, vehicles. Generally not personnel because it has a fairly narrow explosive effective. It is designed to penetrate armour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What is the significance of this information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons carried by these militia are clear violations of the Vance Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page 7460, you testified about the problem of hidden weapons. And if we look under item 5 - we have to scroll down a bit, I think - we see it states, "A lot of weapons in hidden storages." Is this consistent with your information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2844, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Brigadier, did the RSK political leadership offer any official justifications to UNPROFOR for maintaining a large special police force?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary justification was that they were concerned about the Croat forces re-entering the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could take a look at 65 ter 5218. This is tab 153.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the interruption. I see a transcript problem there with the word "concrete." I don't think that was what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be Croat, Croatian, or Croat forces re-entering.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is a memorandum from General Nambiar dated 30 July 1992 and addressed to Mr. Goulding. First of all, did you attend any meetings with Milan Martic in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But not this particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at the meetings that you did -- attended how did Mr. Martic portray his authority over the RSK police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic claimed to be the ultimate political authority in the Krajina that all arms of the government were responsible to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now you -- you said Mr. Hadzic. Did you mean Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you'd actually got that wrong but --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the question is about Mr. Martic, then he -- he was the military police authority working to Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This memorandum reports on a meeting with Milan Martic regarding disarming and disbanding the militia forces. And if we look under item 2A Martic is reported as stating that there were 7.000 regular militia and 16.000 special purpose militia which were the minimum requirement to counter the threat of infiltration and terrorist attacks by the Croatians. Was Mr. Martic the only member of the RSK leadership who insisted on maintaining a special police force of this size?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special police were deployed throughout all of the four UNPAs. It was a -- a centrally controlled, directed policy that converted military to police. We call them other names. As I indicated yesterday, they were called special police, border police, et cetera. Now at the time when they were going through this process of converting them they were simply saying that these were normal arrangements in the former Yugoslavia to have this -- this number of police in such an area. And then later the justification became that they needed them, these sort of numbers to protect themselves from Croat threat. But initially it was presented that having 22.000 policemen in an area like this was perfectly normal and consistent with policy in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did they present UNPROFOR with any evidence of that historical practice?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not convinced anyway. We believed that it was a gross misinterpretation of the Vance Plan and a deliberate attempt to get around the provisions of the plan and to maintain a military presence. We made representations at the highest levels, unsuccessfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us, where were these special police forces deployed within Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about Serb forces now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about the Serb special police forces, these 16.000.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending upon their function, if they were described as customs police then perhaps they were deployed to the entrances of the UNPAs. Otherwise they were generally deployed around the line of confrontation but also in depth throughout the UNPAs so that they could keep an eye on what was happening in the urban and village areas of the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I believe you testified yesterday about the various names that these special police were called, and you've referenced it just now, customs police, border police. To your knowledge, were any of these special police forming a law enforcement duty?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have taken it upon themselves to perform such a function but there was actually another group of policemen who I would call municipal police whose function was routine law and order function as we would understand it. But the special police would sometimes involve themselves in applying justice within the communities which -- which I would call harassment, intimidation, but they would have another name for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall whether these special police forces or -- or portions of them were deployed outside of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I may come back to that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But if we could tender this into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2845, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Brigadier, yesterday you testified, and this is at transcript page 7460, line 16, that members of the special police were engaged in ethnic cleansing and violence, and I think you have also referenced that today. Based on the information you received, could you tell us some examples of the types of crimes these special police were committing in the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base my observation on reports that I read in UNPROFOR headquarters by -- or reports submitted by police officers in their chain of command, and, to a lesser extent, from the Military Observers. But the form of harassment or intimidation included, murder, beatings, robbery, rape, destruction of property.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And against whom were those crimes committed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 1207. This is tab 34. This is an UNPROFOR military information dated 24 July 1992. And we see CMO listed under info. Would you have received this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have had the opportunity to have read it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 15. Now, under Sector East, it reports that the militia and special police are involved in threats, robberies, et cetera. How often would you receive reports of these types of crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout all of the four UNPAs virtually daily in one form or another. It would be rare that you would see evidence of a concerted campaign throughout the whole of the Krajina usually isolated incidents but many of them in a week, probably at least some daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was done with this information that was gathered by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many cases, the allegations were investigated in depth by the police, a full dossier was prepared, handed over to the relevant legal authorities with a request that action be taken. Inevitably no action was taken. In other cases, they were simply reported up through the chain. In other cases, UN were deployed in the area where a particular family might be threatened but it was never possible to -- to be able to protect every individual within the UNPAs from such activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may, Brigadier, I suppose that it goes without saying that when you say the allegations investigated in depth by the police, you mean the regular civil police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, by the UN police in the absence of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: UN police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: UN police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was this information brought to the RSK authorities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, on a regular basis, at all levels from the local level to the highest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think you've mentioned this before but did the situation ever improve in 1992 or 1993 with regard to these crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't, which indicated to me that there was no great desire by those in authority to stop this practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could quickly turn to page 7. And I'm interested in the last ... if we could scroll up to the top. I'm interested in the first paragraph at the top but the last sentence which is pertaining to Sector South. We can see that on the previous -- the prior page. But it states: "The TDF do not support the plan of keeping arms, weapons and equipment inside the UNPA and favour the storage inside the pink zone." First of all, could you just tell us what is TDF standing for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Territorial Defence Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We will be taking about the pink zones in a bit, but what was the significance of the Territorial Defence storing weapons in the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they did that, they would largely be unsupervised by the UN. They would be retained within the pink zones but not under UN supervision. If they came outside the pink zones then they had to go under the lock-and-key process.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2846, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to return to 65 ter 1212.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is the UN Secretary-General report from 27 July 1992 that we looked at for a bit yesterday. I would like to turn to page 5. And if we could look under paragraph 15. The report mentions the expulsion and a number of other crimes being committed against non-Serbs and the direct or indirect involvement of the police in these incidents. You had an opportunity to review this report. How does this information compare to the information you were receiving from the field?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It accurately reflects the circumstances within the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look at the next paragraph, paragraph 16, it states: "All such criminal acts had been protested vigorously by the Force Commander and his staff with authorities in Zagreb and Belgrade and with the local authorities, but there has yet been little visible improvement in the situation." Is that consistent with your observations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, although to say "all" might be just a little bit ambitious. That's -- the author may have exaggerated it slightly there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 7 of this document. I'm interested in -- I believe it's Section D, paragraph 23. A little bit while ago I asked you whether any special police forces were operating outside of Croatia. Could you take a look at this paragraph, 23, and see if that refreshes your recollection on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. The question was about police. This, in part, sort of refers to the TDF which was mainly that force which was demobilised supposedly handed in their weapons but was allowed to remain within the UNPAs. They would be from time to time mobilised by the Serb authorities, they would re-arm themselves, and they would carry out defensive or offensive actions around the UNPAs. Now, to me, it's sort of semantics in a way because sometimes it's the TDF and sometimes it's the police that were performing the same function.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could look at the penultimate sentence. It mentions Bosnia-Herzegovina. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've absolutely no doubt that there was close co-operation between the Serb forces in Bosnia and those in the Krajina. They certainly were working to a centrally co-ordinated military strategy and there would have been very close co-operation if for no other reason than certainly logistics. And from time to time when there was a particular crisis, troops were moved from one end of the Krajina to the other, and in some cases they were, I believe, helping the Serb forces in northern Bosnia. In some cases, the Bosnian Serb forces were helping the Krajina forces over in Sector South against Croat activity. So there was -- while they were supposedly separate entities, they, in fact, worked as one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we tender this report into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2847, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Brigadier, we've spent some time now on the special police. Could you give us your impression of overall how serious of a problem these special police posed to the security situation in the Serb-controlled areas of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the root cause of most of the problems within the UNPAs. They -- they were the agency through which intimidation and ethnic cleansing was affected. They were absolutely central to all of the UNPROFOR's difficulties in carrying out its mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 3624. This is tab 43. This is a further report of the Secretary-General pursuant to Security Council Resolutions 743 and 762 dated 28 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I note for the record that this is the final and complete draft of a document that was previously admitted as D70.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 11 and if we could look under paragraph 34, we see it states: "The root cause of the deterioration in the United Nations Protected Areas since late July has been the Knin authorities' decision to create new paramilitary forces." We see sometimes in UNPROFOR reports reference to "Knin authorities." What is meant by that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're referring to the political, the Serb political leadership of the -- of the Republic of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And which paramilitary forces is this report referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a combination of Serb territorial forces and their special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we raise this issue with -- with the Defence, whether we could simply substitute this final version of -- of this report for the one that was previously tendered. If I understand it, their position is they do not want to substitute at least at this time and therefore we would just tender this report into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just to clarify, the other document that has been admitted is a draft or a previous version that ends up -- it's part of the process of drafting the final, and we would prefer to have both admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2848, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Brigadier, were the special police in the RSK ever demilitarised in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could just look at 65 ter 1310. This is tab 50. This is a -- an UNPROFOR weekly situation assessment dated 14 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm just going to pause for an a moment to make sure that the transcript is working. The one on e-court doesn't appear to be working but the one in the court seems to be fine. If that doesn't seem to cause a problem, I'd like to continue. Your Honour, I think if I just reboot mine, it might ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I tried to do that, but it doesn't work on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is an UNPROFOR weekly situation assessment dated 14 October 1992. And if we could look under item 3, nature of the problems for Sector East, it states: "No indication of demilitarisation of militia, border police and special militia." That was the situation, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2, it states under item 6 -- so at the top, I believe. Yes: "Regional militia is involved in local terrorism and has aggressive activities." You've already talked about their activities toward the non-Serb population. How did the special police behave towards your UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were on -- on occasions uncooperative on occasions provocative. Most of the time they simply chose to ignore the Military Observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2849.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 5180 on the screen. This is tab 148.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a report dated 8 June 1992. Do you recognise this report, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a report that I was required to send periodically to my national authorities so that they could make assessments as to the continuing safety of myself and other Australians who were serving in UNPROFOR at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2. And I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 5 of your report where you write that: "UNMOs are often subjected to intimidation and threats from local militias who have very loose command structures." First of all, what did you mean by "local militias"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a combination of the TDF which remained within the UNPAs and also the police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what do you mean by "loose command structures"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that it was not clear that the individual soldiers or police were within an effective and tight command structure and were in many ways unsupervised in what they did and were allowed to get away with quite significant breaches of the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were these problems raised with anybody?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general atmosphere, counsel, that these matters were raised as I've indicated before from the local level to the most senior political level on a regular basis, and they continued for the full two years I was there. There's clearly no determination to stamp this sort of activity out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2850.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday we took a look at the Vance Plan, and we saw that it envisioned that UNPROFOR was to prevent the flow of armed forces and weapons in and out of the UNPAs. Why was this a significant task to the peacekeeping mission?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was necessary to remove all of the tools of violence out of the area so that a peaceful environment could exist for the civilian population and to create an environment that would allow the return of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was UNPROFOR able to establish complete control over the UNPA entry points?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly had deployments on the entry points to the UNPAs but these were frustrated by -- quite often by the activities of the Serb forces and they were clearly able to circumvent them because they were able to move heavy equipment around the UNPAs without the UN being aware of it. See from time to time reports of heavy weapons being within the UNPAs for more than a year after they were supposed to be gone. The fact that they were observed means that the Serb forces had established ways of hiding and moving stuff about, despite the efforts of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall where in particular the problem of controlling the entry points was particularly acute?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Batina bridge had a particular reputation for being a difficult area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who or what at Batina bridge was causing problems?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a Serb customs post there which caused some of the problem. On one particular occasion I think there was actually a question of physical violence between the UN check-point there and some militias. I believe they were Arkan elements. Sometime in, I think it was 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 3053. This is tab 124. And this is an UNPROFOR weekly situation assessment dated 4 November 1992. And if we could look under item 3 for Sector East. Assessment states, and I'll just summarise, that BelBat's proposal to withdraw militia CP 500 metres away from the Batina bridge seems to have created tension; that the milicija started to block the road between Sarvas and Nemetin as a result of UN blockade in Batina, Ilok, and Erdut bridges; that the hiding of heavy weapons near the Batina bridge has been observed; and that milicija attempts to recognise the bridges as international posts and insists to take the duty. Can you provide some insight into these issues?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not intimately involved in this particular event. I was reading reports like this and similar ones from my military observers but I was not involved in the management of the response. I'd simply say that this document here reflects my understanding of what was happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And why was there a push to move the police 500 metres from the bridge in Batina?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe for two reasons: One was that when they were co-located with the UN force they were disruptive and provocative; and secondly, it was the UN's responsibility to control access of military and weapons into the UNPAs, not the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And based on the information you received, were these police who were stationed at or near the bridges involved in preventing contraband or armed persons from entering Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding at the time is they were there to facilitate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, we tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2851, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'll ask the same question I've asked regarding other issues, is whether these border control problems were raised with anyone in the region.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. At -- at -- I believe this incident here in particular was -- or the incident involving the physical violence with the Arkan elements was raised at the highest levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was the -- the problem of controlling entry points ever revolved in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, was the issue of freedom of movement important to UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was absolutely essential. You can't do your job unless you're able to move about freely, in fact, unexpectedly so that can you turn up, for example, to search for weapons or to ensure the security of an element of the civilian population. But the Serb forces constantly sought to, in one way or another, control or frustrate freedom of movement by various ruses and attempts to require the submission of patrolling plans, inspection of ID cards, et cetera, et cetera. These were clearly not in any way in accordance with the agreements the parties made in regard to the Vance Plan and were part of a centrally co-ordinated effort to frustrate the work of UNPROFOR. We never really in the time that I was there ensured that there was free unfettered UN access at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could look at 65 ter 5192. This is tab 150. And if we could scroll down a little bit. This is an UNPROFOR sitrep dated 24 June 1992. If we look at the margin on the left side, towards the bottom, can you confirm that you received this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. CMO was marked on the distribution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2. And I want to look at item B, freedom of movement. And this item discusses an incident in which a local police officer stopped an MP patrol and informed them that they needed to notify the local police before starting their patrol. Could you tell us, in what way this kind of incident was a violation of UNPROFOR's freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Effectively the request here is that the UN should forecast their movements and presume that, at least on occasion, when we went to the local police station to inform them about our starting patrol that they would deny permission. The UN has to be able to go, whatever the day or time or night where it needed to go to carry out it's function without being restricted in its movements in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 3 of this document, since we have it in front of us. And if we could look under 7 (a), we see there's report of the Serbian Territorial Defence refused to withdraw tanks from Trpinja. And under item 7 (b)(5), if we scroll down a little bit, it reports that in Darda the first use of a blue painted M60. Could you tell us what is an M60?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't really know. I'm aware of M60 tanks which is a US tank. My best guess it would be some form of armoured personnel carrier or small armoured car produced in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it mentions that it's painted blue. What's the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a heavy weapon or regarded as a contraband piece of equipment and the Serb forces are endeavouring to make it a legitimate sort of weapon of their police by painting it blue rather than green. But it's still -- it's part of this argument they had that police forces in the former Yugoslavia were routinely equipped with heavy weapons and that there were substantially more police available in all areas of all different types, much larger numbers than the Vance Plan or UNPROFOR ever anticipated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2852, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And again I'll return to my -- my question but with regard to freedom of movement of UNPROFOR, was this raised with the RSK political authorities in 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about this particular incident or freedom of movement in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In general.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On many, many occasions at all levels, from the local level to the highest political levels, including President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Since you raised the issue, when a violation of UNPROFOR's freedom of movement was -- occurred or was observed, was it reported generally or on an incident-by-incident basis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each incident was reported and protested, and, from time to time, the central issue was taken up at the higher levels to try and improve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And yesterday at transcript page 7434, you testified about a meeting you had with Mr. Hadzic in mid-1993 regarding the issue of freedom of movement of UNPROFOR. And if we could have 65 ter 5371 on the screen. And this is tab 181. This is an ICFY report dated 3 May 1993, and the report describes a meeting between ICFY representatives and Mr. Hadzic and Misa Milosevic. Did you attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2 and focus in on item number 2. It reports that: "Brigadier Wilson raised the question of UNPROFOR's freedom of movement, particularly in Sectors North and South. On this, Mr. Hadzic commented that once he returned to Knin this would be dealt with in a favourable way [sic] to UNPROFOR." Is this the meeting you were referring to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall who was impeding freedom of movement of UNPROFOR at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the detail at this range. My understanding was that the Force Commander, then General Wahlgren, asked me to raise the matter with Mr. Hadzic, and I did this. And Mr. Hadzic, as indicated in the report, said he would do something about it and my belief is there was temporary improvement as a result of Mr. Hadzic's intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2853.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Besides RSK armed forces and, of course, JNA until they officially withdrew, were there other armed groups operating in the UNPAs in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were elements like Arkan and various other people, names like the Red Berets or the White Eagles. There were a number of different militias, or whatever they might be called, who were able to move with apparent freedom throughout the whole of the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How were they able to do that, move throughout the UNPAs unhindered?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, particularly early -- early in the peace when the Serb forces were still controlling the movement within the UNPAs, they openly carried arms - I'm talking now about a group like Arkan's forces - and they would move through check-points without any attempt to supervise or control them, and I therefore assumed that they had freedom of movement and authority from the highest levels to be able to move through the area armed. Local police forces and militias would simply wave them through. Later, when the UN was controlling movement, they -- they would be less blatant about displaying their weapons but they -- they would still move through the area in their uniforms and at that time with the continued co-operation of the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what kind of activities were these groups that were coming in and operating in the UNPAs engaging in?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reports indicated that they were involved in harassment of the civilian population, activities like smuggling, looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at a document, 65 ter 1824. This is 108. Looking at the subject heading, this is an UNPROFOR update dated 10 October 1993. Who sent this update?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us what -- what were the purpose of these types of updates?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to look at the contents of it, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just generally. Is this a one-off update or is this something that you would send on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look at the contents, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Fair enough. Why don't we then turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. This is an example of a daily report which was prepared within the International Conference for the former Yugoslavia, and its purpose was to update the co-chairman on operational developments within UNPROFOR's area of responsibility in the previous 24 hours. They were done at least daily. Sometimes if the situation was tense or there was a particular issue in UNPROFOR, it would be done more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look under - I'm just checking the paragraph, yes - paragraph 1, you describe an incident in which Arkan's troops forced their way across Batina bridge despite the efforts of BelBat soldiers. You alluded to an incident a moment ago, is this the incident you were alluding to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time I incorrectly said it was 1992. It was clearly 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And why did you feel compelled to include this incident in your update?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was a significant event that forces had actually come to physical contact with each other and it was a very provocative and gross violation of the agreements that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did UNPROFOR or the representatives at ICFY raise this incident with the RSK political leadership?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Are you aware of any action that was taken at the local level with regard to this situation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2854, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 5460. This is tab 189.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is an UNPROFOR update dated 22 October 1993, and it's sent from Colonel Peeters. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a liaison officer from UNPROFOR headquarters who was deployed -- he and a small group were deployed to Geneva from Zagreb in early October, I believe it was, 1993, to perform the function that I had previously been forming as liaison officer to the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn the page. By -- are you saying by the 22nd of October you are no longer UNPROFOR liaison for the ICFY?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Technically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this document looks similar to the one we just looked at at least in format. Is it the same kind of procedure that was being followed by Colonel Peeters as you had performed prior to leaving that position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look under item 1, it is noted that President Hadzic accompanied by Arkan entered Baranja apparently for the participation in the session of the Krajina parliament in Beli Manastir. Is this the same or is it a different incident than the one that you reported on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I believe it's the same. And just curious that they'd be referring to an incident on the 11th of October when the report was written on the 21st or the 22nd of October. But I wasn't the author, so I don't know why they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2855, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How were the borders of the UNPAs determined under the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: By negotiation with the party, but defined in the report as particular "opstina" or parts of "opstina" and listed in detail in the report in the -- in the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did the UNPA borders go all the way to the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't and that created areas which became known as the pink zones. That's an area between the actually confrontation line and the borders that were defined in the Vance Plan as the UNPA boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were UNMOs deployed in the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. An additional force of observers was sent to UNPROFOR to enable this to happen and their task was to patrol the pink zones and ensure that they were demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to return to 65 ter 1212 which has already been admitted. And it's been admitted as P2847. Again, this is the UN Secretary-General's report from 27 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 and if we look under paragraph 10, the Secretary-General reports that Security Council Resolution 762 recommended the establishment of a joint commission to oversee and monitor the process of restoration of the Croatian government's authority in the pink zones. Did the RSK political authorities agree that the pink zones should be restored to the Croatian government's authority?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't. They were impeccably opposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was their position regarding the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were Serb areas that had been liberated with blood and they would never hand them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 5156 on the screen. This is tab 146. This is an UNPROFOR sitrep dated 9 May 1992. And under item 1, the sitrep reports that a mean -- that at a meeting between both Mr. Hadzic and Minister of Defence Spanovic: "They took forceful position on UNPROFOR deployment within administrative rather than ethnical boundaries in Krajina. They stress that, as a result of this, JNA, Territorial Defence, and police units have the obligation to defend almost 50.000 Serbs to be abandoned between UNPA's boundaries and cease-fire lines and they are not going to withdraw from their positions unless UNPROFOR moves there." Brigadier, were any Serb armed forces in fact present in the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. I think, counsel, we have to keep in mind this is May 1992, and UNPROFOR didn't assume responsibility for the UNPA in Sector East until June, I believe. So this reflects a negotiating process between the local Serb authorities and UNPROFOR to establish the boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after that process was complete, could you tell us, what types of Serb forces were in the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- my belief is that they were one form or another of police forces. And there were TDF elements who were not openly armed but they were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2, and I think if we look at -- I think it's probably the third dash down. It reports that Mr. Hadzic and Spanovic stated: "Even if JNA gets order to withdraw most of its officers and men will stay and join the TD or police units to fight CA because up to 95 per cent of JNA personnel here are locals." Did this in fact occur, this absorption of former JNA personnel into local forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in theory, both in the Krajina and in Bosnia, this was the position that the JNA withdrew and with all its forces and all its personnel. But we know in reality that they -- they didn't withdraw fully at all. They continued to provide personnel, logistic support, direction, and various other forms of support. But this was part of the well orchestrated, centrally controlled, centrally scripted plan to circumvent the Vance Plan and to avoid honouring agreements, was done at the highest level - one suspects under the direction of Milosevic - but carried out by his people on the ground, including Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one clarification. When reading this part of the report, you said that men will stay and join TD or police units. Brigadier Wilson, could you please look at that part of the text and tell me what TD means or is it something else that is written there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does state TD, Your Honour, and TD refers to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2856, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 1367 on the screen. This is tab 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is an UNPROFOR memorandum from General Nambiar to Mr. Goulding dated 14 November 1992. And if we could turn the page, we can see that this memorandum attaches a translation of a letter from the RSK state committee for co-operation with UNPROFOR sent to the UNPROFOR Force Commander and the Deputy Force Commander. Were you aware that this committee for co-operation existed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, I may have at the time, but I don't recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You didn't have any direct interactions with them.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 6, and if we could look at the second paragraph on this page, the committee writes that: "On a several occasions we proposed the correction of borders of the protected area to take into consideration at least the actual situation when our positions are in question." And if we could then go to the third paragraph, the committee goes on to write: "If this proposal were accepted, the Croatian refugees would return to the territory in which they represented ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Try again, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Testing ... I think it's resolved, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So we're looking at the third paragraph. The committee goes on to state: "If this proposal were accepted, the Croatian refugees would return to the territory in which they represent an ethnic majority and where the Croatian authority is functioning and the Serb refugees would go back into their ethnic area where the RSK authority is in jurisdiction." From the perspective of UN peacekeeping, did this type of proposal present any issues?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible to act upon because the only way that boundaries could be changed was agreement between the parties and that's effectively the responsibility of the co-chairman, not UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR couldn't possibly facilitate -- such an agreement would be done at the very highest levels, probably between Presidents Tudjman and Milosevic. This is wishful thinking, perhaps delaying, obscuring the facts, whatever you wish, but it's a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What would have been the practical effects of this proposal of moving the boundaries and allowing certain refugees to enter into Serb-controlled areas and other refugees into Croatian areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I couldn't speculate on that without knowing the detail of the particular map and numbers and history, et cetera. It's not just not possible to comment on that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Fair enough. If we could turn to page 3, and if we look at the third paragraph on this page, the committee writes that: "At all joint commission meetings, your Military Observers," presumably, UNPROFOR Military Observers "report that the Croatian side is the only one violating the cease-fire." This letter is from November 1992. Is that a correct assertion as to the situation in November of 1992 with regard to cease-fire violations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's a gross misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2857.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Based on the information you were receiving from the field, what was happening to the Croatian population in the pink zones in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were being harassed, intimidated, encouraged to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was happening to their houses?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases, they were destroyed after they left. And in some cases, they were damaged while they were still residing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 3052 on the screen. This is tab 123.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is a slight addendum to that answer. In some case they were being, once vacated, occupied by Serb refugees from other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. If we could have 65 ter 3052 on the screen. This is an UNPROFOR weekly situation assessment dated 28 October 1992. And if we could look under nature of problems in Sector East, I think it's the fifth bullet point or dash down, it is reported: "Increased number of Krajina custom officers and milicija are observed at Batina bridge." I think you've alluded to this before, but was there a legitimate customs service operating at this time period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't know the answer to that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to page 4. And we can see at the top, it's reported: "The destruction of Croatian houses inside pink zone continues mainly in the zone number 2 and sometimes in UNPA too." Was that the situation in the pink zones, based upon the information that you were receiving?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall, based on the information you were receiving, who were the perpetrators of these kind of crimes against the non-Serb population in the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on reports that I saw, it was in many cases carried out by the Territorial Defence force or the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2858, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR make any demands on the RSK authorities with regard to the removal of Serb armed forces from the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe there were many protests sort of made to the Serb authorities where there were clear violations of the agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did the RSK authorities withdraw these forces from the pink zones while you were working in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it's accurate to say they attempted to minimise their position there rather than to remove them. They would camouflage weapons or take uniforms off but still, in effect, remain there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could look at 65 ter 1799. This is tab 102. This is an UNPROFOR daily sitrep dated 23 September 1992. And if we look at the bottom of the page, can you confirm that you received this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My title is on the distribution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 8 and look at the section on Sector North. It's reported that: "Regional commanders said they have no order to discuss any withdrawal of special milicija from the pink areas." Is that consistent with your recollection of the situation in the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's one of the excuses given. It's just a delaying tactic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2859, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You've already testified regarding crimes committed against non-Serb population, including them being forced from their homes. How often would you receive reports regarding expulsions in the UNPAs while you were CMO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Explosions," I'm not sure what you mean by that term, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I used the term "expulsions." I suppose you could also use the term, as you use it, "forced from their homes."

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand you mean were properties blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No. Reports of people expelled from their homes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it was routine. I can't say it was daily but it was certainly least weekly. You'd get reports of that sort of activity.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Brigadier, I'd like to show you another document that's in the same vein. If we could have 65 ter 5934 on the screen. This is tab 212.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, this is an UNMO memorandum dated 22 April 1992. Could you tell us, who is forwarding this information to DCA Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR headquarters. It's not my signature. So I'm -- sorry. It was the UNMO headquarters, within UNPROFOR headquarters. A lieutenant-colonel signed it but it's not -- it's not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And he signed it on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that was within procedure? He could do that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perfectly normal. Unless it was a matter of policy or a significant document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2. Unfortunately, we don't have a collection of UNMO individual reports. Would this be an example of -- of -- of perhaps early on an UNMO document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's unusually brief. To be honest, they would normal be more fulsome.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next page before we talk about the substance. And there is a full -- it's handwritten but there is a full report that -- that -- that follows. Was it unusual for reports to be handwritten at this April 1992 time-period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite common. We were still assembling the resources we needed to do the job, and computers and typewriters were in short supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And perhaps if we turn to page 8. And we see at the bottom, we see signatures. One is of an UNMO Osijek official and the other one is -- it looks like a BelBat official. Was that common for them to submit joint reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. Without reading the report in detail, I'm not sure why they would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's -- I don't want to spend a tremendous amount of time on the content of this memorandum. I think if we turn to page 2, it more or less summarises what its contents is. And I think we see it says: "Hereby a report of events on 20 April 1992 concerning expelled-refugees from Tenja, Marinci and Vukovar." And then it mentioned that UNMO, looks like 21 and B1 were present. They arrived in -- looks like 2-sector. I'm not really sure, I can't really read the handwriting. And then item 2 states: "Please inform B-HQ and HQ UNPROFOR in Sarajevo to take necessary steps." What would be the necessary steps when a report such as this regarding expulsions was sent up the chain?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an expectations that higher authority would protest or demand some corrective action would be taken, but it was presenting the evidence so that higher commanders could take some action.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2861, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter 5204 on the screen. This is tab 152.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a cover memo. If we could turn to page 2. And now we see on page 2 a daily sit report -- sitrep from HQ UN CIVPOL Sector East dated 10 July 1992. And looking at the left-hand margin, were you a recipient of this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3. And we'll -- this -- this page should suffice. But we can see that the document reports on a number of crimes committed against non-Serbs; for instance, the first one is a -- is a murder. The section actually relates to a detainee, and the one after that deals with looting, it appears. Was this the sort of the information you were receiving from the field regarding criminal activities in the sectors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's typical.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were the local police responsive to these kind of crimes when they were informed about them from UN CIVPOL or other UNPROFOR organs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was they were uncooperative.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2862.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, what was happening to non-Serb religious buildings in the UNPAs and pink zones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of them had been destroyed or at least damaged prior to UNPROFOR's arrival. But destruction continued throughout the period 1992/1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you personally witness any of this destruction?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I certainly witnessed the effects, not the actual destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you give an example where you did -- I know you didn't see the actually destruction of that but where you witnessed the results.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall in 1992, early 1992, going through a village in Sector North which had many destroyed houses but an intact mosque. On a later visit to my Military Observers there I noticed that the mosque had been destroyed by an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us what level of destruction was it with regard to that mosque? Was it still standing or was it reduced to nothing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parts of it were still standing, the minaret had largely been brought to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Based on your experience as a military officer, were you able to assess the amount of explosion -- explosives that would have been necessary to -- to cause that kind of damage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- I couldn't guesstimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 3622. This is tab 137. And this is an UNPROFOR military information summary dated 9 September 1992. And if we look under info, can you confirm that you received this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 22, I believe. And if we look under Sector South, towards the bottom, it is reported that: "Extremists actions have increased and all are aimed at destruction of Croatian houses and Catholic churches?" Brigadier, did this kind of destruction of religious property follow particular events?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it appeared it was at random and rarely a whole series at the same time, usually isolated incidents, although I think there was a period when I was in Geneva that there was a concerted effort to destroy places of worship and there was a higher level representation made to ask that this cease. I'm not quite sure of the exact date but I do remember there was wave of destruction. It could have been in September of 1992, when there was the push from the Croatian government for the return of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified that there was a higher level, I believe, representation made to ask for this to cease. Who was that representation directed to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was Mr. Thornberry writing to the Krajina authorities. Whether that was Mr. Hadzic, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Since we're on this document, if we could turn to page 6. And if we could look under item number 2 of the entry for 31 August/1 September. The summary reports that letters were sent on 1 September 1992 to Mr. Martic protesting strongly against two attempts at refusing UN personnel freedom of movement. Was that the practice to send these types of letters?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. But to different people from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2863, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen 65 ter 5256. This is tab 162. And we see -- or if we could draw your attention to the left-hand margin. Did you receive this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you comment on what occasions you would receive an individual report from a sector opposed to what we've been looking at largely, which is UNPROFOR-level reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we received copies of the -- all sector reports came in and my staff processed those and prepared a daily briefing for the Military Observers' headquarters. That briefing preceded the Force Commanders' conference so that I was broadly aware of what the operational situation was before attending the Force Commanders' conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2. And if we could look at item C. It's reported that terrorism is going on, and then lists damage to seven Croat houses, as well as an attack on Catholic church in Draz. Is this an example of the information you were receiving regarding property destruction?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a typical report of 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And since we have this document in front of us, if we could look at the next item, I think it's item D. The reports -- speaks about an incident in which a BelBat APC ran over an anti-tank mine that appeared to have been deliberately planted on the road in Sector East. Were you aware of similar such incidents involving your own UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In early 1992, while I was still deployed in Sarajevo, one of my Military Observer's vehicles was subject of a similar incident, where they drove over an anti-tank mine placed on a road that had previously allowed for clear passage and safe passage. Somebody had deliberately mined the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what happened to your officer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was very badly wounded, lost lower part of one leg and had to be repatriated to his home country.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2864, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You -- you testified a moment ago about the unresponsiveness of the local police when crimes against the non-Serb population were reported to them by UNPROFOR organs. I'd like to show you 65 ter 5296. This is tab 170. This is a report, an UN report on the situation of human rights in the territory of former Yugoslavia prepared by the Special Rapporteur of the Commission on Human Rights and its date is 17 November 1992. And if we could turn to page 24, we see at the bottom, begins a section on -- section A on United Nations Protected Areas. And if we could just turn the page, to 25, the sections continue and they cover the various -- the four UNPAs. Did you have an opportunity to review these sections on the UNPAs before you testified?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to paragraph 78. And this is under the section dealing with Sector South. And it reports that: "The courts are still not functioning properly and the investigative processes of the local police have, in the opinion of UNPROFOR officials, almost ceased to exist." Did you share that assessment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was this only a problem in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It applied in all of the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was your assessment of what was at the root of the local police's failure to prevent and investigate crimes against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the absence of an effective command of chain -- a chain of command and it was an absence of direction from higher authorities to make sure that normal policing, normal safe environments were established in the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was this issue of a lack of law enforcement raised with the RSK authorities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood -- understand it was raised with them on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned, I believe it was last session, that Serb refugees were occupying Croat homes in the pink zones. Did this occur elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Also within the UNPAs proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page -- I think it's the next page. Yes, and if we could focus in on paragraph 84. It in fact, discusses the issue of placing Serb refugees in empty houses for those who fled sector -- the empty houses of those who fled Sector East. What impact did this bringing Serb refugees into empty houses of Croats have on the -- the implementation of the UN peacekeeping plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it -- it changed the ethnic composition of the area. Made things like having a -- a representational or in proportion to all nationalities in, for example, the police force virtually impossible. And it was an attempt to, I guess, establish facts on the ground that would affect the ultimate political settlement. But the reality was that these Serb refugees had -- had also been forced to -- to leave or elected to leave other locations and needed somewhere to leave. These were empty houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2865, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You have testified about some events relating to the BelBat, the Belgian battalion that was based in Sector East. How would you evaluate the performance of BelBat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: BelBat was a very professional military unit. It would have been one of the best battalions in UNPROFOR. And because it carried out its work professionally, there was a lot of tension with the local Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall how the RSK political authorities reacted to BelBat's activities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
