utterances.text: I believe they wanted them withdrawn and not replaced with another Belgian battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall Mr. Hadzic's view on this issue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he wrote to the UN expressing exactly that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 1275. This is tab 40. And I'm interested in the article that begins on the bottom right, an article by Belgrade "Tanjug" dated 25 September 1992 and the article reports that Mr. Hadzic stated that he agreed with the idea that withdrawal of the Belgian battalion from Baranja be requested as urgently as possible because of the troops' improper behaviour and the problems they make for local authorities. In what way had the BelBat troops behaved improperly, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe they had acted improperly at all. They had acted professionally in accordance with their mission and with the mandate of UNPROFOR. They had attempted to hold the Serb authorities in the area accountable for their actions. They had attempted to honestly restrict the movement of the armed elements and weapons, and this had caused great tension with the Serbs at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2866, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How important to the UN peacekeeping plan was the return of non-Serb refugees to the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the mission of -- of UNPROFOR was to help create an environment that would allow for the eventual return of Croat population to the UNPAs. Sorry, I lost track much the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You more or less answered it. I was asking how important it was to the mission?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ultimately, it was central.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the Croatian government's position regarding returns?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were insistent, impatient. They wanted it to happen before there was a political settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was the position of the RSK political leadership towards returns of -- of Croats?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was widely expressed that the two nations couldn't live together again and that separation would need be to set in concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 1336. This is tab 55. And this is an UNPROFOR military information summary. It's dated 2 November 1992. And if we look under the info section, can you confirm that you received this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 5 of the report. If we could look at item D, Sector South, the summary reports: "The local milicija are ready to deploy to deny access of any Croatian coming back into the Serb-controlled areas." Were you aware of these types of deployments or plans for deployments in the event there were returns?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the whole period 1992 to 1993, there were regular threats from the Croat forces to invade the UNPAs. This was quite unsettling for the environment. Kept the Serb authorities on edge. It was destabilising for the local population and led to reports like this where the Serbs were ready to deploy forces to counter a perceived threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now this reports that they are being deployed to prevent the returns not to prevent an invasion by Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says "any Croat coming back." It's ambiguous, in my view whether it's talking about military action or return of refugees. Same thing. The threat to return refugees or military action had the same destabilising effect upon the environment in the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look further down under Sector South, it is reported: "The training of new milicija is likely to continue if not checked." What was the concern about the training of new milicija?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm unfamiliar with this particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 10 then. And if we look at the top of the page, we see the -- we see reference to a -- two 120-millimetre MOR (BUM-52). What -- what is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are 120-millimetre mortars. They're a heavy weapon. It's in clear violation of the agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look under the 28th of October, down towards the bottom, 1B, the UNMO reported: "Erdut 1 blue B VP/M80A at milicija HQ." Then it says: "This is a violation of the Vance Plan, and may even be considered as a provocation because the location is only a few hundred metres away from SHQ." First, what is a B VP/M80A?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's an armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And why could the location of this vehicle a few hundred metres from SHQ be considered a provocation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: SHQ is the sector headquarters and they are effectively saying we are aware that this is a violation and it's here anyway and you can't do anything about it. It is highly provocative. It's arrogant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2867, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Brigadier, were you aware of the discovery of a mass grave in Ovcara in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when did you first learn that there had been a massacre at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the -- the period of UNMLOY prior to the deployment of UNPROFOR. When travelling around with Croat liaison officers they alleged that there had been a massacre of patients from the Vukovar Hospital during the war and that there was a mass grave somewhere in Sector East.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you recall when during your mission, your UNMLOY mission? Was this towards the beginning, the middle or end, as far as when you received this information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very early in the process. So mid-January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 5282 on the screen. This is tab 168. This is a military information summary dated 26 October 1992. And it's a bit hard to read, but if we could zoom in -- yes. Under info section. Can you confirm that you received this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 1992, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. It's 26 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would have received this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 6. And if we look under 17/18 October 1992, item 3, the summary reports: "The reconnaissance of a possible mass grave near Ovcara ... was conducted by sector staff, UN CIVPOL, and a representative of UNHCR." And the site is being guarded by RusBat. Why was it necessary to post guards at this site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To secure a crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was that within the mandate of -- of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2868, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Brigadier, we've, through the course of your testimony, talked about a number of impediments to UNPROFOR's mission: Freedom of movement, border control, lack of demilitarisation, et cetera. Based on all those factors, what conclusions did you arrive at regarding the RSK authority's attitude towards the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that prior to UNPROFOR's deployment in former Yugoslavia a plan was worked out and -- to be carried out or directed from the highest levels to negate, wherever possible, the -- the Vance Plan and to avoid compliance, to set up means of bypassing processes, so that the circumstances on the ground would in no way diminish the Serb control of the area and the prospects for long-term retention of the areas they captured during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at 65 ter 5294. This is tab 169. This document is dated 15 November 1992. Can you tell us, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my end-of-tour report to my national authorities on completion of my time as Chief Military Observer in UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3 of this report. You summarise the UNPROFOR operational situation in Croatia, focussing particularly on the role of the local police forces. And I think that is a consistent with what you were saying early, that they were a major impediment to the mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you conclude with the remark at the end of the paragraph: "The political leadership is clearly responsive to directives from Belgrade and actively opposes UNPROFOR's attempts to fulfil its mandate." Now, who were you referring to when you use the term "political leadership"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the entire Serb leadership from President Milosevic down through the political leadership of the Serb Republic of the Krajina, down to the local level. It's the total organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2869.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, did other members of the UNPROFOR leadership share your view that the RSK political leadership or -- and even higher, the higher levels of leadership, was actively opposing UNPROFOR's attempts to fulfil its mandate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this was a unanimous view, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How would you describe your superior, General Nambiar, as a Force Commander?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Highly professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how well did he understand the situation in the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 1349 on the screen. This is tab 60. What we have in front of us is a coded cable from General Nambiar to Mr. Goulding dated 8 November 1992. Do you recognise the signature to the right of the document number, UNPROFOR 8-290?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. That's General Satish Nambiar's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Under paragraph 1, General Nambiar writes: "It is amply clear that notwithstanding all their assurances of co-operation and support for the Vance Plan and other associated Security Council Resolutions, the Serb authorities in the UNPAs have implemented only those aspects of the plan that suited them and have blocked progress on further implementation to gain time for furtherance of other political and military objectives. In effect, they have managed to use our deployment and presence to get the Croatians 'off their back' in the UNPAs, thus enabling them to intensify activities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They have also used our presence to consolidate their rule in the pink zones, and have been terrorising and seeking to drive out remaining Croatian residents, usually very old people." General Nambiar uses quite a few words but how does this compare to your assessment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's much more eloquent than my evidence but I agree with it entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 2, he lists as an option a chapter 7 enforcement action. What would that have entailed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have had a lot of implications, but ultimately it would mean that UNPROFOR would have had to fight the local forces to impose its will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At this stage, was that a likely scenario to actually to be achieved?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is extremely difficult to transition from a peacekeeping force where you are lightly deployed on the ground into an effective fighting force. It requires retraining, re-equipping, reorganisation, redeployment. Extremely difficult to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2870, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to play a video for you. This is P2328, tab 145. And if we could just display it but before playing it for the witness. Sir, do you recognise the person who is facing us in this initial image?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person on the left is Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could now play the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... useful for the Serbian people, but ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could we re-start it and play it again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "My views is that this Vance-Owen Plan should be accepted, not because it is useful for Serbian people, but because it is not achievable. As a friend of mine, a high-ranking Serbian politician from Republika Srpska said - I can even mention his name - Momcilo Krajisnik - he said, and it is now funny, but also a bit sad, because it clearly a misunderstanding: We cannot accept this plan because it is not feasible. Let Vance and Owen, Izetbegovic and Boban think about it, but we should have accepted it and showed the the world we are for peace and continue to hinder this plan and do our job of organising Serbian countries because it is obvious the world does not recognise the war anymore. We saw how the terrorist in France was treated ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We heard Mr. Hadzic state that he suggested to Momcilo Krajisnik that we should accept the Vance-Owen Plan "and show the world we are for peace and continue to hinder this plan and do our job of organising Serbian countries." How does this suggestion during this interview compare to how you and other UNPROFOR representatives perceived the RSK's leadership's attitude towards the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated earlier, we believe there was a centrally directed preconceived idea to circumvents the Vance Plan and to frustrate it in any way possible. This is a media statement of probably an understatement of what they intended to do. I believe this view was shared with other key personnel within UNPROFOR headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified that in December 1992, you were redeployed to the ICFY as -- well, two hats: Military advisor as well as UNPROFOR liaison officer. Could you tell us - I don't believe you had an opportunity to before - what were your primary duties in those positions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They varied over time. Initially, I was ensuring there was a flow of information from UNPROFOR headquarters to the co-chairman and also in the other direction, so the Force Commander would know what progress was taking place at the conference. It was also from time to time various proposals with about military aspects in the negotiations which I offered advice on the feasibility or otherwise of implementing those proposals. Later, when Mr. Stoltenberg replaced Mr. Vance, he was appointed the Secretary-General special representative and effectively the Force Commander then reported to New York through Mr. Stoltenberg. At that time my task as military assistant became more important and I was helping with the -- Mr. Vance along with Mr. Stoltenberg's interface with the Force Commander in the headquarters to make sure that he was able to perform his role as the Special Representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified that one of your responsibilities, at least initially, was to ensure there was a flow of information from UNPROFOR headquarters to the co-chairman. Were you in this position kept informed of events, problems that were occurring in the UNPAs, even though at this point you were no longer CMO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was very well informed. I continued to receive the daily situation report, and I also received a copy of all critical correspondence between UNPROFOR headquarters and UN New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 1696. This is tab 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Again, I asked for 65 ter 1696. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is an UNPROFOR weekly report to SR SC. I'll repeat, this is an UNPROFOR weekly report to SR SC dated 3 July 1993. And we see, if we scroll down a little bit regarding distribution, BGR JW. Who is that referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 14 of this document. This is a civilian affairs briefing note for Mr. Annan. What was the purpose of these kind of notes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To keep Mr. Annan, who was then the Under-Secretary General for peacekeeping operations informed of developments and the situation in UNPROFOR. But it's a report from the civil affairs officer, Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look under item 4, we see a briefing note regarding the various sectors in Croatia. And it states that in Sector East, there has been an escalation in attempts to control UNPROFOR movement. In certain villages minority Croats are under pressure from the milicija and other local bodies to leave their homes. Croatian men are also being arrested and charged with having served in the enemy army or having conducted armed rebellion against the RSK. Is this information contained in this report consistent with the type of information you were receiving in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you continue -- I think you did mention at the beginning of your testimony that you continued to visit the UNPAs in your capacities with the ICFY on one or two occasions with the -- with the co-chairs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. But they were usually by air so there was less opportunity to observe what was physically happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you -- from what you could observe, what could you see? Had the situation dramatically improved in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same or it got worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In December 1992, did you attend an ICFY conference in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many conferences in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. Let me focus your attention. A conference at which the acting US Secretary of State Eagleburger was present?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I believe that was the 16th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who from the Serb leadership do you recall was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was a large forum of all persons associated with the peace process at that meeting from President Tudjman, President Izetbegovic, President Milosevic, and the Serb Krajina leadership, namely Mr. Hadzic, were present at that meeting, and many of the military commanders, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were there any representatives from the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. There was Mr. Karadzic and some of his other political leaders, and General Mladic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did acting Secretary Eagleburger give a speech?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did. He gave a very forthright, very blunt speech in which he said to everybody assembled there that he was well aware of the war crimes, the ethnic cleansing, all of the nasty stuff that was taking place in the former Yugoslavia, and who -- who was doing it. And they would be held accountable for it. I believe that address he was foreshadowing the creation of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Brigadier, what were the primary negotiations that you attended in 1993 relating to the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very broad question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Maybe I can try to narrow it. Can you -- I know you attended quite a few negotiations during that period. Let's take, for instance, negotiations in New York. Did you participate in those?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The reality, Your Honours, most of the negotiations, serious negotiations, in 1993 in Geneva were concerned with the Bosnia-Herzegovina situation because it was recognised that you couldn't solve the other problems until you'd solved that one. So -- but on the side of those meetings there were other issues discussed, like what was happening in the UNPAs, and there were ambassadors there from the conference who were chairing those particular meetings. Now I participated with Mr. Ahrens from Germany. He held ambassadorial rank for negotiations on the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And other than Ambassador Ahrens, who else were among the chief negotiators with regard to the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: These matters were addressed in passing by the co-chairman but their focus was on Bosnia. It was really left to other people within the conference to try and move other negotiations along. Certainly Lord Owen, Mr. Stoltenberg, Mr. Vance addressed what was happening from time to time in the UNPAs, but their focus was on solving the Bosnia problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To what degree were the international negotiators, Ahrens and others, aware of the human rights violations that were occurring in the Serb-controlled areas of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were fully aware of because they were receiving the same information that I was. They were recipients of the daily report that I wrote for the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did they raise these issues with anyone during negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us among the RSK leadership who they raised it with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to be specific here, Your Honour, because the passage of time and also there were so many different meetings, so many different conversations, I can't possibly recall the detail of every meeting and conversation. But what I can say is that ethnic cleansing, the harassment of the population in both Bosnia and UNPAs was a fact of life and something that had to be dealt with by the negotiators. It was the context in which they were dealing. So it was discussed often and at length with all parties at all different meetings, not necessarily at every meeting but certainly anybody who attended the conference as a negotiator would have been exposed to the sort of warnings and the conversations about the unacceptability and the existence of this sort of conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How often was Hadzic present at the ICFY negotiations that you attended regarding the conflict in Croatia, in other words the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am guessing that I was involved with Mr. Hadzic about half a dozen times, maybe a bit more. There were negotiations held both in Geneva and also in New York at UN headquarters. It may have been more or less, but about six I would guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at those meetings that Mr. Hadzic was present at, do you recall his responses when these human rights violations were raised?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. In broad terms it was the usual response from the political leadership that uncontrolled elements, provocations from the Croats, they're doing it to us. It's impossible to stop this sort of activity. Generally not accepting responsibility for what is going on but finding excuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 65 ter 1750.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's 12.15, Mr. Olmsted, next break. It will be at 12.15, I mean. Not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Oh, yes, absolutely. Yes, we're moving along, Your Honours. And just so you know, I may go a few minutes into the next session but I'm almost complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 1750. This is tab 97.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Your Honours, may I tender into evidence 65 ter 1696. It's the last document we looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2871.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is a letter from RSK prime minister, Djordje Bjegovic to the UN Secretary-General, and it is dated 22 August 1993. I think if we can turn to page -- page 2 we can see at the bottom that it's from the prime minister of the RSK. And I am interested in the fifth paragraph which is a little bit difficult to read. It's -- yes, it's the penultimate paragraph. And it states, "As for Mr. Valentic's assertions," and I believe he is referencing the prime minister of Croatia as -- that's who Valentic was: "As to Mr. Valentic's assertions of ethnic cleansing, persecutions, and killings of the non-Serb population within the UNPA zones, one has to wonder when these three-year-old reiterations will cease, because if summed up, Krajina would understandably [sic] be a nation of ghosts." What can you tell us about this kind of statement at -- at this stage, August 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't reflect reality because ethnic cleansing continued, in my experience, between -- well, during 1992 and 1993. They're not old allegations; they're current.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2872.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wanted to think about whether I want to go into the next area at all. If we could break now, I might have an answer when we get back. It's a new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll take the second break now, Brigadier Wilson. We'll come back at 12.40. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I do have one brief topic. I don't think it's going to take more than five, ten minutes, maximum. If we could have 65 ter 1862 on the screen. This is tab 113.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you tell us, what is this document.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my end-of-tour report after my assignment to Geneva. It's to my national authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2. I want to focus on paragraph 9, at the bottom, yes. And in this paragraph, you are writing about negotiations to resolve the conflict in Croatia which you state have been characterised by the extreme and diametrically opposed positions of the parties. What I'd like to focus your attention on is a little bit further on you write: "The Serbs insist on the right to form their own Republic, to be later linked with other Serb territories (Greater Serbia)." You're talking about negotiations here. Could you tell us, who espoused this view among the Serb negotiators?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't attribute that to any individual. I -- I think it's a general impression that I had of all of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2873.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would now like to show you a brief video-clip. This is 65 ter 1332. This is tab 54. And we are going to start at around 41 minutes and 10 seconds, and I have an image still on the screen here. Brigadier, could you identify the persons here.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left is Mr. Karadzic, and on the right, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And now if we could -- this is going to be page 14 of the English transcript. And if we could play -- play the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We're just waiting from -- an indication that the interpreters are ready. I believe we're ready now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Here in Prijedor Serbian history is being made. There are two presidents of the young Serbian republic. First, President Karadzic. Thank you very much, Mr. Hadzic. The declaration has just been adopted. You participated yesterday in this august act. This is a great step for the Serbian history, a great step towards the unit of the Serbian people. We have proven that this is the unified interest of the Serbian people ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's try playing it again because the transcript doesn't conform to what's in the English translation. It seems we are missing a few parts of it. Maybe -- maybe it's difficult to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Here in Prijedor, Serbian history is being made. Here are two presidents of the two young Serbian republics. Who should we hear first? President Karadzic. "Radovan Karadzic: Our guest first I think although he is no longer a guest in this. "Reporter: Thank you very much. Mr. Hadzic, the declaration has been just adopted. You took part in this discussion tonight. You attended the formal ceremony. "Goran Hadzic: This is a great step for the unity of the Serbian people, and I think that this is the first time step to the final unity of the Serbs. We have already demonstrated before, but since London definitely, since the London Conference that the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina have the same interest and the adoption of this declaration is only a logical step towards the unification of all Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Brigadier, during this clip, we a hear Hadzic saying or referring to the unification of all Serbian people. How does this compare with what you recall was the position being made during negotiations with the ICFY?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is consistent with what was raised in the ICFY.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2874.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. President, that completes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Brigadier Wilson, thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. If I may for the record indicate that we're joined today by Jolana Makraiova, our legal intern. If I could also just say for the Registry that it appears e-court has gone down at least on the terminal in front of me. And it now seems to have returned. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Brigadier Wilson.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Gosnell. I represent Mr. Hadzic here and I'm going to have a few questions for you today, going over to tomorrow, I'm sure. If any of my questions aren't clear, please feel free to ask me to clarify. If you get tired - I know you may have some jet lag - then please feel free to mention that and I'm sure it can be accommodated. Now you testified yesterday at page 7430 for my learned friend that "I personally never witnessed anybody being ejected ...," and that's referring to non-Serb civilians from the protected areas, "So I'm basing my evidence entirely on reports that I received from the ECMM or from UNPROFOR sources or from Croat sources." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And does that statement also apply in respect of the individuals who you have been able to identify as perpetrators in your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, I never observed anybody evicting anybody, nor anybody being evicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So that the extent you're able to identify any of those perpetrators or their affiliations that's based on the underlying, ground-level documentation that you received; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's reports -- based on reports from a wide variety of sources, additional resources to the ones that I gave in my evidence like the media and NGOs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, you've told us there were special protocols about the verification of information that was contained in UNPROFOR reports from which I would expect that you would place primary reliance on the UNPROFOR reports, including the CIVPOL reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And, of course, you would cross check reports between each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And to the extent that what you've been able to testify to here orally, differs from what is contained in those underlying reports, would I be correct in understanding that you would defer to the underlying reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the reason I ask that question is because when one reviews the underlying reports from UNPROFOR and from CIVPOL sources, one does see, on occasion, more than on occasion, references to milicija, either local or regional being involved in crimes, but there's also a wide variety of other descriptions. And those descriptions include -- I'm going to give some references here just for the record but I won't pull them up. The references include unknown terrorist groups, that's P2851, page 3; paramilitary group, P2859, page 4; armed uncontrolled troops, 3054, page 3; uniformed men sometimes masked, carrying automatic weapons, 1353, page 3; and in 1141, armed bandits, unknown persons, ten unknown soldiers, unknown persons, and four armed men with military uniforms? Now, what I want to ask you is about your understanding of the term "special police." Did you understand that the term "special police" was some kind of catch-all category that it would include all of these various descriptions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I'm personally referring to special police it's a collective description of people who presented themselves as police but under different titles. You've given a -- a list of descriptors in reports, I have say many of them sourced from non-English speakers. There's a lack of standard terminology within UNPROFOR. It depends upon the time-frame when more accurate definitions became known. If you look in March, June, at reports, they'll be quite different to those later in 1993 when the organisation was a bit more sophisticated and there was a greater knowledge of what was going on. So a lot of the different terms that are used is, I believe, a result of throwing together an organisation that has never really worked together and a lack of standard operating procedures. But getting back to your question, when I am talking about special police I'm talking about people who present themselves as policemen not these other armed elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you accept, it seems, that in the protected areas there were other armed elements other than the special police.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And who were they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were people who we -- we described as milicijas. These were people who had taken off their uniforms but you were still part of the TDF who could at short notice respond to security threats. They would access weapons which were largely hidden from the UN and perform a military function.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The court reporter has just asked that you lean forward a little.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So are you then saying that there is a Territorial Defence force which is existing concurrently with the special police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Any other groups or individuals armed and present in the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there were elements of the JNA who were not -- who were disguised and I believe there was indeed a change of forces between Bosnian military organisations in the Krajina. They were not necessarily discreet. They co-operated and operated in each other areas as required.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what about civilians who possessed long-barrelled weapons but who were not part of any particular formation? Did that exist in the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt that there were such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Wasn't the UN's estimate in 1992 that 70 per cent of the population in the protected areas was armed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unaware of that statistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does that accord with your impression and your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I couldn't put a percentage, but I'd say many of the male population would have been -- would have had access to weapons. They -- it was quite commonly known that the JNA had gone through a process of arming civilians before they withdrew, both from the UNPA and also from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You testified a page ago, page 69, that you referred as being special police those who presented themselves as special police. Do you allow for the possibility that there were individuals claiming to be special police, in order to give them -- themselves the entitlement to carry rifles?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And they certainly would have had a motivation to do that when stopped by anyone from UNPROFOR who would otherwise threaten to take away their gun; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some individuals might choose to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could have P2869, please, which is Prosecution tab 169. And this is your report of the 15th of November, 1992, which is towards the end of your role as commander of the monitoring mission. And if we could go, please, to page 3. The description that you give here is that there are various militias emerged on the JNA withdrawal under the guise of police forces. And then you go on: "Despite the presence of the Serb 'police ' and 11 UNPROFOR battalions there has been a total collapse of law and order. Ethnic cleansing and all associated with it continued and is, for the most part, conducted by 'police,'" again in quotation marks, "forces." And then down at the bottom the last sentence is: "Further, UNPROFOR attempts to fully disarm the militias have been unsuccessful." Now, I read in that, that you seem to perceive some level of - dare I use the word - Balkanisation within the category, described as police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say there, counsel, is that before the demilitarisation process started in the UNPAs, there were a large number of armed militias. A proportion of those, 16.000 of them roughly, were converted into police, which I'll call special police. That left some other thousands who, under the Vance Plan, were to take off their uniforms, hand over their weapons to either the UN or the JNA, as the JNA withdrew, and to allow UNPROFOR to provide security in the area. The reality is that those -- most of those militias in fact remained in place, simply took off their uniforms but had access to weapons and acted -- still continued to act under central control and respond to specific security threats and directions from a higher authority. But they were, if you wish, undercover militias. In addition to that, there is the police force of some 16.000 who I say in my report and I stand by that, were the agents of harassment and intimidation of the central authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you don't accept the possibility that most of or even a significant percentage of the harassment and intimidation was being done by individuals off their own wicket?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do accept the fact that some of these -- this harassment and intimidation would be on individual initiative. But my observation was it was such wide-spread throughout the four UNPAs and was over such a long period of time, that it was an orchestrated campaign and that if the Serb political authority disagreed with it, they had two years and 22.000 policemen to fix the problem, and they failed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So from a failure to stop it, you infer a plan.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe they had the means to stop it, if they truly wished to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you say that you would draw the same conclusion regardless of whether the perpetrators then are special police committing crimes while on duty, special police off duty, or armed individuals not within the structure of the special police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that primarily because in the many, many cases where fully presented dossiers were presented to the legal authorities about these crimes being committed by a variety of individuals, be they civilian, militia, or police, the authorities failed to act upon those.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You've testified earlier that the local police were, in your view, or shall I put it -- put it more accurately, your recollection of the documents were uncooperative; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in respect of that judgement, would you defer to officials who were on the ground in place of yours if they gave a contrary opinion about the level of co-operation of local police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what officials you're referring to, counsel, but there are people clearly more qualified to talk about police matters than I am. I was the recipient of police reports. I had discussions with very senior police officers. I have a general sense of what was going on but if you wish an expert then I'm not an expert in police matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: Do you recall based upon either the documents or any conversations you had with others in UNPROFOR that there were virtually no cases where UNPROFOR or CIVPOL was able to identify the perpetrators of the crimes against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that. I'm aware of certain situations where the name of the individual was known and was a repeated offender and the -- the legal authorities within the Krajina failed to take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That wasn't my question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My question was isn't it the case then in the vast majority of cases, and I accept that there are exceptions, but in the vast majority of cases the identities of the perpetrators were not identified by UNPROFOR or CIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in many cases wasn't that because the perpetrators deliberately tried to conceal their identities when they committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many reasons why individuals are not able to be identified. There was no witnesses or witnesses are too scared to give evidence. Lack of access for the UN, lack of co-operation. Many, many reasons. But it's true that in the vast majority of cases perpetrators could only be identified perhaps in the most general terms like uniformed or un-uniformed, or carrying weapons or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you remember that the reports the indicated that a great many crimes were committed either at night-time or by individuals who deliberately concealed their face?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me shift gears, Brigadier, and ask you some questions about the Vance Plan specifically, if I may. Could we have P2794, please. And if we could please have page 5. This, Brigadier, is the historical background document which I believe is from 1994 but it does contain a copy of the Vance Plan in annex. And here is part of the Vance Plan. And paragraph 7 gives the basic concept, and it says: "These areas would be demilitarised; all armed forces in them would be either withdrawn or disbanded. The role of the United Nations troops would be to ensure that the areas remained demilitarised and that all persons residing in them were protected from fear of armed attack." Now, if I understand your testimony from yesterday correctly, the obligation or the role of protecting all persons residing in them, or of all persons residing in them being protected from fear of armed attack never became operational because the various steps that were collateral with the Vance Plan were not achieved. Do I understand that testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we could just turn back to page 2, we see there the five steps. And we can all read them. I'm not going to read them out. But may I just ask you this question: What heavy weapons did Croatia possess at the end of 1991 or early 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they -- they had artillery, tanks, some aircraft, a range of -- of weapons, but they were not as well equipped as the JNA were, nor as heavily armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What kind of artillery pieces did they have?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't know. I would guess a selection of weapons from the JNA inventory, because all of these weapons were stored throughout the whole of the Yugoslavia and they would access them when the war broke out or perhaps before that, so they had -- they had a reasonable quantity. But I can't tell you exactly how many, but less than the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm not so much interested in the quantity but I am interested in knowing what was the heaviest calibres, the largest calibre heavy weapon, and you were the head of the UN monitoring mission, what was the largest calibre piece of artillery that Croatia had at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine something like 155 artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the range of that is about 5 kilometres in terms of accurate targeting; is that correct or am I understating it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's more like 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So that means under step 1 Croatia is only required to withdraw the heavy weapons ten kilometres out of change of the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it says 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Correct. And if 155-millimetre Howitzer gun has a range, an effective range of 20 kilometres, that means that they're required under tep 1 to withdraw 10 kilometres out of range, out of their effective range?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If they fired they would be landing 10 kilometres short. Thirty kilometres is selected because it exceeded the range of most, if not all, heavy weapons of the former JNA. There were some missiles that certainly the Serb forces had, I don't think if the Croats had any, that would exceed 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And amongst the other requirements here are that anti-aircraft, systems, anti-armour weapons, heavy machine guns be withdrawn to a distance of 10 kilometres and that infantry be withdrawn to a distance of 5 kilometres from the protected areas. Let me get right to my question. If the Croatian army decided it wanted to conduct a Blitzkrieg type operation against the protected areas, given the amount of distances to which they had been required to withdraw, how long would it take them to move into the protected areas in days or hours?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in -- it depends on -- if you're talking about the whole assault it would take a number of days, but the buildup of such a force would be readily apparent to any number of observers casual and otherwise who are operating on both sides of the confrontation line, it's not really practical to assemble a large military force easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you whether or not it would go unnoticed. I'm asking you, as a military man with many years experience, if you were starting, if you were commanding a force, starting from these positions, how long would it take you to move into the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would take hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, in return for being given hours' notice of an attack that would overrun all the protected areas, what did the Serbs get in this Vance Plan deal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, in simple language, can you describe for us what the Serbs got out of the Vance Plan and what the Croats got out of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They got what they both agreed, they both accepted. They both reached some sort of compromise, be it their political, military, security or whatever else, they both signed up to and agreed that they would honour and enforce the Vance Plan. They got what they wanted. Otherwise they would never have agreed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So the Serbs -- if we can turn over to paragraph 7 again, or to page 5. In your view the position is that the Serbs have agreed to entirely demilitarise the protected areas, give up any protection whatsoever, and in return for that, even before the Croats have withdrawn to the lines set out in the five steps, where is the protection for the protected areas during that period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have agreement between two parties which hopefully they'll both honour. I mean, there is an agreement brokered by Mr. Vance with the highest political authority of both parties that they won't attack each other, that they will respect a cease-fire. There is effectively in the plan a separation of forces. It doesn't completely negate the possibility of either side using force but what it does do it reduces the possibility of accidental clashes or accidental action because there is a separation. If one side is determined to circumvent the Vance Plan, then the Vance Plan is not going to work. And I have given considerable evidence about this. And now if -- if you want me to say did the Croats ever violate their side of the agreement and attack the UNPAs, yes, they did. But fundamentally we're talking about agreement that essentially neither side respected 100 per cent. They got exactly what they deserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What I'm trying to get at is -- is wasn't it the original concept of the Vance Plan that in return for the JNA withdrawing from the protected areas, that UNPROFOR, with its infantry units, would then serve in the role of protecting those areas from incursions by Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the plan. And that's what everybody wished would happen, in particular UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I think you have been very clear about this, that was, on the one hand, the role that they were expected to fulfil but, on the other hand, there's no authorisation to use force in case of an armed incursion, is there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is. It says in the Vance Plan that force may be used but essentially limited to self-defence but it does not exclude the probability of using force to carry out the mission, and indeed on occasions the UN used force and I was witness to it. That they were able to use force but it was never intended that the UN would be able to stop a major assault by the Croatians into UNPAs because there was an agreement. Why would this happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, there was Miljevacki Plateau which I'm sure you're very familiar with, and the Chamber is familiar with it, which occurred in June 1992, and then there was the Maslenica bridge incursion which occurs in January 1993. Now, in respect of those two events am I right that there was no response in terms of a military response from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge, there were two French soldiers killed in Maslenica in that action, counsellor. Whether they were caught in the middle or whatever, but certainly if you're asking me to say did the UN try and push these people back, no, it didn't because that was never envisaged as their responsibility, but did the UN take vigorous diplomatic and response and bring political pressure to bear, yes, they did. Was it effective in achieving with a withdrawal of the Croat forces? No it wasn't. This was the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And there was almost non-stop - and you've mentioned it earlier today - pressure from Croat forces around the confrontation lines on the Serb side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not entirely correct. I would say that the Croats were more active in some areas than they were in others. Some parts of the former confrontation line were very quiet. Some were more active. And I would say it wasn't all of the time that such pressure existed. I would say from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have P2211.2168, which is Defence tab 62. Let me just first ask you about -- this is a status report from Sector South dated the 7th of September, 1992. If I can just ask you about the first line: "UNPROFOR's mission is still in a military phase. Stalemate in wdl process at step 3/phase II ..." Can you help us understand what that means?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I believe he is referring to those five steps we saw earlier in the -- in the Vance Plan, but I'm not the author of the document so I'm guessing here. And he is saying that the -- the complete demilitarisation as of September 1992 is not yet achieved, in particular, I believe, he says on the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we can turn now to page 3, please. Croatian military option: "Risks of military action to restore Croatian authority are indeed realistic. "Croatian side's patience and good will is reaching the point of non-return. They seem to react out of pure nationalism. October is a deadline for them and therefore a turning point for the whole operation. "Provocation/retaliation process is intensifying. Pressure on the front line from Croatians increases daily under form of incursions, infiltrations of both armed groups and civilians." Now from the information you had in September 1992, did you think that there was a Croatian military option to commence incursions against the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier in my evidence that September 1992 was the time when the Croatian political leadership were vigorously agitating for the return of refugees. And I said earlier that this was highly destabilising for the UNPAs. And the UN was doing everything they could to tone down this rhetoric but it was -- nevertheless, it was provocative and there was posturing along the UNPA borders by Croat forces in this time. There was a great deal of tension in September/October of 1992 and it's true, in particular, in the area of Sector South, that the Croats were very active along the UNPA border. I believe this reflected their concern that this -- this occupation by the Serb military forces there was interfering with their ability to communicate north/south on the Croatian coast and it was highly destabilising for them. So that's the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What did the posturing consist of that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as indicated in this report, there was patrolling activity, clashes, firing across the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And infiltrations, forces moving into the protected areas and --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I mean by patrolling, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, given these circumstances, and I'm asking you now to take off your UNPROFOR hat and put on your military-man hat, wasn't it perfectly reasonable for the Serbs to say, Just a moment here. UNPROFOR doesn't have until all five steps are satisfied the obligation to protect the protected areas, and, on the other hand, here come the Croatian forces over the borders of the protected areas. Now, given that situation as a military man, wasn't it reasonable for the Serbs to decline to completely disarm?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a central issue. This is a -- but it's a chicken and the egg argument. It's a circular argument. If both sides had honoured the agreement there wouldn't be this situation. Now we have the situation, the agreement's no longer valid, and therefore people start arming themselves. The root cause of the situation is the parties did not honour the agreements that they signed up to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree with me that the demands on the Croatian side are fairly modest. There is no request for disarmament or demilitarisation. All that's required is that they move their heavy weapons beyond the 20-kilometre firing range for their heavy weapons and that they move their infantry 5 kilometres back. Fairly modest obligations on their side, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection of their discussion at the time was they were agitated that they had territory that they thought was sovereign, Croat territory that they were not allowed to occupy, that their population had been forced to leave. They felt they were giving up an unreasonable amount. That was what they put to the conversations that I observed and took part in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you remember also that one of the central tenants of the Vance Plan that final status of the protected areas was supposed to be a matter of negotiation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And yet notwithstanding that that was the provision in the Vance Plan, you're saying that the Croats still refused to withdraw to the relatively, I suggest, modest, bench-marks that are set out in the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying that they -- they did comply but they were guilty of violations. If you want to look at from a legalistic point of view, the reality is that they circumvents the agreement that they signed on to. Both sides failed to honour the agreement and made the situation unworkable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But from the Serb perception of things, and you suggested this earlier, those non-compliances would be -- would create fear, to put it simply?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 01831, please, which is Prosecution tab 109. Now this is you writing to Mr. Stoltenberg and Lord Owen in October 1993 and I believe the context here is the discussions about the extension of the UNPROFOR mandate. You say here: "Further, for understandable reasons, they have refused to disarm their forces." What did you mean there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's reflecting the facts on the ground in October 1993 that there was a serious threat to the Croats -- to the UNPAs and that it is understandable that because of that threat the Serbs would take some actions to protect themselves. It is logical, understandable but not endorsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And from a military perspective, reasonable?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a military -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, if I can just take -- have us focus on the first line there in paragraph 2: "The Serbs have rejected S.C.R. 871 and all aspects of previous resolutions which challenge their claim to independence from Croatia." Now you were asked quite a number of questions or a few questions, shall we say, about what the Vance Plan meant for JNA forces. And we're certainly clear, that at the least it required them to withdraw in Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, or Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And with the recognition of Croatia as a state, a return of the JNA or later the VJ, as it came to be known, would be an act of aggression against a foreign state, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Whereas, if the Croats decided to break the Vance Plan and move into the protected areas, they would just be reclaiming their own territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, did it ever occur to you or did you ever hear expressed from the Serb side that one of the central reasons why they wanted independence or some level of international recognition was precisely to provide a bulwark, a protection, against precisely that possibility?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you hear it expressed during the negotiations by the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On many, many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now you've told us your view that UNPROFOR's obligation under paragraph 7 of the plan would not be operational until satisfaction of all the five steps. That's your interpretation. Was that the officially UNPROFOR view, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I don't know, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, you were a senior member of UNPROFOR. You were involved with all the senior leadership. You don't know if the official view was that UNPROFOR did not have the obligation to step in and deter an armed incursion should it occur in the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the question was did I consider that UNPROFOR had been successful in carrying out the plan. That was the question. That's how I interpreted it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, maybe I should be clearer because I know my questions -- the last two were long. But was it the official UNPROFOR view that they had no obligations under paragraph 7 until the five steps were fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I dont' think that was an official position. I believe we've seen where the Force Commander, General Nambiar, wrote to Mr. Annan expressing his concern about his inability to -- this is in September, I think, of 1992 to fully carry out the mission and he lists the reasons for that. Now, in the interim, UNPROFOR is actually on the ground and is endeavouring to do what it can to assist the parties to honour an agreement they both made, and where appropriate and where they had the ability to do that, then they would intercede. But it was never intended that a peacekeeping force would stand between two warring parties. It's a monitoring mission that's designed to supervise an agreement and to assist the parties to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And General Nambiar would have told the Serbs that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have D70, please. Prosecution tab 44. I'm sorry, I'm reminded that I did not tender the document that is on the screen. I would like to do so, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D91, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this is from a -- well, this is a further report of the Secretary-General pursuant to Security Council Resolution 743. May I ask you, do you know how these -- I assume the Secretary-General himself is not personally drafting this report. How does a report such as this come into being, based on what you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR headquarters would be asked to provide the basic information, perhaps even an early draft. It would be written mainly by Mr. Thornberry, the director of civil affairs with considerable input from the Force Commander. In the case of General Nambiar, in the case of the latter two commanders that I worked with, Generals Wahlgren and Cot who were not native English speakers, they would have had to rely on other people. That information and that draft would be sent to the office of the Under-Secretary for peacekeeping operations, who was initially Mr. Goulding and then later Mr. Annan, and the -- the person within that organisation who would probably do the draft would be a political officer by the name of Shashi Tharoor, an Indian diplomat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That last name is T-h-a-r-o-o-r.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry. The spelling on that is T-h-a-r-o-o-r. If we could turn over to page 4, please, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this is discussing the justification for the special police as it was perceived by the interlocutors with the Serb side from UNPROFOR. It says here: "The justification given by the Knin authorities for these forces is that they are needed to defend Serb-controlled areas from attacks and infiltration by the Croatian army. General Nambiar has repeatedly stressed to the authorities in Belgrade and Knin that it is UNPROFOR which exercises the protection function in the UNPAs and that the presence of these paramilitary units is contrary to the United Nations Plan and has caused the Croatian army to retain some of its forces at the confrontation line." Now, you've been very clear about your position but what do you think General Nambiar -- would have been the content of General Nambiar's assurance to the Serb side in terms of the protection function? What do you think he promised or what do you know that he promised to the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that. I'm sorry. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And while we have this document on the screen, could we please go to the next page: "Despite the passage of the deadline for the first stage of this process, however, demilitarisation has not begun. The authorities in Knin, who nominally control these elements, have stated they cannot comply with the agreement," et cetera, "because UNPROFOR cannot control the situation." Do you know why this report describes the control as nominal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. If you want me to guess it was because from time to time there were claims that there were uncontrolled elements. The Knin authorities would say these are renegade, uncontrolled elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is the Secretary-General's report so obviously it has been accepted to some degree of satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to object to that. I raised this issue earlier. This is a draft of the final report. I'm -- I haven't compared the language, but to represent that this is the report when it is only a draft, it's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: 3624, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Which is the final report, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Page 3, paragraph 9, at the bottom: "Despite the passage of the deadlines [sic] ... demilitarisation has not begun. The authorities in Knin, who nominally control those elements, have stated that they cannot comply with the agreement because of Croatian army behaviour and the alleged inability of UNPROFOR to control the situation." Does that assist you at all? I received an objection from the Prosecution and I'm sorry to have to put the question again to you. Does it help you understand?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is the question about nominal control?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I can't really speculate. I perhaps incorrectly gave you a guess. The true answer is: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This document is already admitted so I don't need to tender it. Could I have 01367, please, Prosecution tab 65. And it's now P2857.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You looked at this document, sir, earlier. And if we can turn the page over to page 3. And this is Mr. Zecevic writing to General Nambiar. And just on page 2 he starts by saying: "We also believe that you are very much aware of the reasons why we agreed to the Vance Plan."

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's not on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I apologise. Could we just have the bottom of page 2, please: "We also believe that you are very much aware of the reasons why we agreed to the Vance Plan." And then we turn the page: "In spite of that, we think it should be repeated that the basic reason for accepting the Vance Plan was a total security of the population in the protected territory provided by the presence of UN troops." And then he quotes paragraph 7. Now -- and then he goes on in the next paragraph: "This provision of the Vance Plan was the main reason to accept it. In my deepest conviction, this provision expresses the very essence of the Vance Plan and this is why we insisted on it in all our contacts with the representatives of UNPROFOR." And then the penultimate paragraph: "Likewise, we insisted on having your answer and guarantees for complete realisation of the obligation under point 7 of the Vance Plan, and no adequate response has been given, least of all a positive one." Now, do you remember that the Serb representatives were expressing the view that this was their interpretation of the Vance Plan and that they considered the obligations in paragraph 7 to be immediately operative?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that situation at all. Quite to the contrary. They were constantly telling us that they had to provide security because we couldn't. Wasn't so much that they were insisting that we should implement the Vance Plan. They were saying that we were not doing it and therefore that's why they retained arm, that's why they created all these police forces. In fact, really before UNPROFOR got there they were anticipating this situation. So I -- I just regard this correspondence as posturing, counsel. It's not -- doesn't seriously represent the bulk of communication that existed between the Serb authorities and UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
