utterances.text: You don't think he is being genuine in saying, Listen, we signed up to the Vance Plan. We agreed to the demilitarisation. We agreed to opening our doors, in a sense, contingent upon that protection being provided. You don't think that was genuine and sincere?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, counsellor. I believe there was a premeditated plan to circumvent the Vance Plan and to apply any of those aspects that suited the Serb side, and I think we saw evidence of that earlier in the clip from -- video-clip from Mr. Hadzic which he said was quite deliberately going to accept it but we'll do our own thing anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And yet you testified earlier that it was reasonable that they didn't disarm.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was militarily understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You see, what I'm getting at and what I want to put to you is that what these documents show, whatever the merits may be, whatever may be the sense of greater good, the Serb side did have a legitimate and genuine reason to have these special police. Even if it might be viewed as a -- not in the compliance with the Vance Plan, they had good reason to set up those forces. Or at least they had a genuine reason to set up those forces other than going out and terrorising the civilian population. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree entirely with your -- your statement, that they had genuine concerns for their security. But I don't know that the course they selected was the best one. There were many other options that were available to the authorities prior to the arrival of UNPROFOR and while UNPROFOR was there. It comes back to the central -- to my central belief that for the whole system both parties had to honour the Vance Plan and neither party did, to the extent it was never possible to create a genuine, secure, unthreatening environment in the UNPAs. Having 2.000 or 22.000 police, it was not necessarily the best solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say it was the best solution. But what I do say is that it was a reaction, justified or otherwise, a reaction to the threats, the real and present threat posed by Croatian forces combined with UNPROFOR not assuring concretely that the UNPAs would not be invaded. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I -- I consider it to be an option. There were other options. I think it's a poor option.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm not -- we're not discussing the merits of the options. We're discussing what the motivations were. And what I'm suggesting to you when we look at these documents, in context, that was -- that was the motivation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said in my evidence and I consistently say it, I believe this was premeditated. This option was selected before UNPROFOR even arrived on the ground. They had decided that they would create a situation which was basically destabilising and threatening. It would neve have been possible under those circumstances for UNPROFOR to have completed its job. It was premeditated, centrally directed, consistent through all of the four UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now you testified yesterday that by the time you arrived in what would become the protected areas, most non-Serbs had already left; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason from a -- in -- in -- given the goals that you've just suggested, namely, undermining the Vance Plan and in order to not demilitarise, how would forcing out the remaining few non-Serbs in any way advance that particular agenda, if at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got absolutely no understanding why people would involve themselves in ethnic cleansing. I'm sorry, counsellor. I just don't understand that philosophy at all. I can't imagine why they would want to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have D71, please, which is Defence tab 14. This is a memo from General Nambiar to Marrack Goulding and it relates or at least it's issue soon after the Maslenica bridge incursion. And the Chamber has seen this document before, so I won't go through it chapter and verse but I would just like you to look at one or two paragraphs. Paragraph 4 on page 2: "There is every indication that he, Tudjman, had or at least perceived he had the tacit support of some members of the internation community. Hence it is most unlikely that he will implement S.C.R. 802 in the correct spirit. I cannot see him relinquishing control of the recaptured territory to anyone, not even the United Nations." At the bottom: "I should also like to draw your attention to the attached agency report on his interview in the current edition of Der Spiegel." Now, what would the consequence be in terms of confidence on the Serb side of assurances of the Croat side of, first of all, this incursion, and, secondly, retaining the territory that was seized as a result of this incursion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would this -- did this operation inspire confidential on the Serb side to disarm?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh no, highly destabilising.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And on the next page: "On the Serb side, as I mentioned in one of my earlier cables, we are seen as traitors and betrayers. This is mainly because we had relied on Croatian assurances of willingness to sit and talk and had persuaded many of our Serb interlocutors of that faith." Basically isn't it the case that right up until this date, UNPROFOR did have to rely on mainly Tudjman's assurances that he wouldn't proceed to invade the protected areas rather than any real obstacle presented by the UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was relying upon the agreement that President Tudjman and Milosevic had signed, the Vance Plan which -- in which Tudjman said he would not encroach upon the UNPAs. Just further evidence that both sides failed to respect the Vance Plan and made it impossible for a peacekeeping mission to -- to observe agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we can go down to page 6, please. You have addressed this subject before, but now this is a different document: "If no international negotiations are to take place, then UNPROFOR should be given either a more realistic and limited mandate, much more resources and a mix of chapter 6 and chapter 7 or it should be removed, but the key, as was the case in Bosnia, is the peace making role." Now is this a recognition by General Nambiar that UNPROFOR has had imposed on it a task it can't perform, an obligation it can't perform unless it has more resources and more authority?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And he is saying, isn't it, that that's a precondition for ensuring that those protected areas actually be protected?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without studying the document in more detail I can't comment on that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Given that this is occurring right after a major Croatian incursion into a protected area, isn't he saying, Listen, we need more resources and chapter 7 authority if you expect us to protect the protect the areas meaningfully.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe what he is saying is the Vance Plan is impracticable, but it ought to be revisited and UNPROFOR should be given a different mission and more resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Brigadier Wilson, this is the end of today's hearing. You are not released as a witness. I explained to you yesterday what that means in regard to discussing your testimony with other people or talking to one of the parties. We expect you back tomorrow at 9.00. And, Mr. Gosnell, I suppose there is no problem in finishing the testimony of this witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I certainly hope not, but there will be some substantial cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Wilson, for today. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
